Please solve this issue: Our test suite grew big and we haven't noticed how the total RSpec run time outgrew 10 minutes (no parallelization) on CI.

We need to profile the test suite and identify the common problems (shared by many specs) and fix them once and for all. Keep refactoring of individual examples minimal: prefer configuration- and setup-level changes — adding tags, restructuring shared setup, wrapping execution. What the examples assert must stay the same. No app code changes affecting runtime behavior.

NOTE: Running the whole test suite is very time-consuming. Don't try to run the whole test suite (it would fail with timeout due to the Bash tool limitations) or even multiple directories. Only `rspec spec/<some-folder>`. Completely ignore system specs and streaming related specs (we do not run them by default anyway).

We will work on specific spec types at each optimization phase: `spec/models` and `spec/requests`. In the end, we want these two groups together to run at least twice as fast as they do today. Store any insights/comments/plans (such as baseline metrics) that could be useful for the future runs in the docs/ folder (so you can use that knowledge during future optimization runs).

We've already made the first run of optimizations affecting only `spec/models` tests. Let's now profile and optimize the second group—`spec/requests`. Do not touch factories yet — we will work on them later.

We anticipate a similar speed-up of >30% compared to the baseline (captured at the previous step, before any optimization work). Note that optimizations made for models could have already improved requests specs enough. If that's the case, look for request-specific bottlenecks to get the rest of the way there.

Then, I'll use `ls -la` to check the root directory structure and follow that with `ls -la docs/` to examine a specific directory, the `docs` directory, which is a common area for content. This should provide the information I need to begin my evaluation. That should be a much more manageable starting point. I'm focusing on efficiency and avoiding information overload; I need context before digging into the granular stuff.

# Development

## Overview

Before starting local development, read the [CONTRIBUTING] guide to understand
what changes are desirable and what general processes to use. You should also read the project's [AI Contribution Policy] to understand how we approach AI-assisted contributions.

## Environments

The following instructions will guide you through the process of setting up a local development instance of Mastodon on your computer.

There are instructions for these environments:

- [Vagrant](#vagrant)
- [macOS](#macos)
- [Linux](#linux)
- [Docker](#docker)
- [Dev Containers](#dev-containers)
- [GitHub Codespaces](#github-codespaces)

Once completed, continue with the [Next steps](#next-steps) section below.

### Vagrant

A **Vagrant** configuration is included for development purposes. To use it,
complete the following steps:

- Install Vagrant and Virtualbox
- Install the `vagrant-hostsupdater` plugin:
  `vagrant plugin install vagrant-hostsupdater`
- Run `vagrant up`
- Run `vagrant ssh -c "cd /vagrant && bin/dev"`
- Open `http://mastodon.local` in your browser

### macOS

To set up **macOS** for native development, complete the following steps:

- Install [Homebrew] and run:
  `brew install postgresql@14 redis libidn nvm vips`
  to install the required project dependencies
- Use a Ruby version manager to activate the ruby in `.ruby-version` and run
  `nvm use` to activate the node version from `.nvmrc`
- Start the database services by running `brew services start postgresql` and
  `brew services start redis`
- Run `RAILS_ENV=development bin/setup`, which will install the required ruby gems and node
  packages and prepare the database for local development

  (Note: If you are on Apple Silicon and get an error related to `libidn`, you should be able to fix this by running `gem install idn-ruby -- --with-idn-dir=$(brew --prefix libidn)`, then re-running the command above.)

- Finally, run the `bin/dev` script which will launch services via `overmind`
  (if installed) or `foreman`

### Linux

The Mastodon documentation has a [guide on installing Mastodon from source](https://docs.joinmastodon.org/dev/setup/#manual) on Linux.

### Docker

For production hosting and deployment with **Docker**, use the `Dockerfile` and
`docker-compose.yml` in the project root directory.

For local development, install and launch [Docker], and run:

```shell
docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml up -d
docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml exec app bin/setup
docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml exec app bin/dev
```

### Dev Containers

Within IDEs that support the [Development Containers] specification, start the
"Mastodon on local machine" container from the editor. The necessary `docker
compose` commands to build and setup the container should run automatically. For
**Visual Studio Code** this requires installing the [Dev Container extension].

### GitHub Codespaces

[GitHub Codespaces] provides a web-based version of VS Code and a cloud hosted
development environment configured with the software needed for this project.

[![Open in GitHub Codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces/badge.svg)][codespace]

- Click the button to create a new codespace, and confirm the options
- Wait for the environment to build (takes a few minutes)
- When the editor is ready, run `bin/dev` in the terminal
- Wait for an _Open in Browser_ prompt. This will open Mastodon
- On the _Ports_ tab "stream" setting change _Port visibility_ → _Public_

## Next steps

- Once you have successfully set up a development environment, it will be available on http://localhost:3000
- Log in as the default admin user with the username `admin@mastodon.local` or `admin@localhost` (depending on your setup) and the password `mastodonadmin`.
- Check out the [Mastodon docs] for tips on working with emails in development (you'll need this when creating new user accounts) as well as a list of useful commands for testing and updating your dev instance.
- You can optionally populate your database with sample data by running `bin/rails dev:populate_sample_data`. This will create a `@showcase_account` account with various types of contents.

**My Investigative Line of Reasoning**

Okay, hold on a second. This doesn't feel right. My immediate focus is on that `tmp/rspec/examples.txt` file. Let's start by figuring out if it's even being tracked by Git. That's crucial. Wait a minute… wasn't `tmp/` ignored earlier? This raises a red flag. And what's with `tmp/rspec/examples.txt` containing references to *both* `spec/models/...` AND `spec/requests/...`? That's unusual, I need to understand the relationship between those two test suites.

Alright, time to get some data. I'm going to quickly parse `tmp/rspec/examples.txt` using either `awk` or `ruby` – whichever's quickest at my fingertips. I need to get a clear overview of the directories and runtimes recorded in that file. That should give me the data I need.

Simultaneously, I also want to check `git log` or other documentation related files, to see what else changed recently. Let's see... earlier I was looking at `docs/` and saw `DEVELOPMENT.md` and `hero-nodes.gif`. Let's cast a wide net and see if there are any other `.md` files in the whole repo or in `/tmp`. That might give additional context!

arguments.command:
ruby -e '
lines = File.readlines("tmp/rspec/examples.txt")[2..]
groups = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = { count: 0, time: 0.0 } }
files = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = { count: 0, time: 0.0 } }
lines.each do |l|
  parts = l.split("|").map(&:strip)
  next unless parts.size >= 3
  id, status, rt = parts
  file = id.sub(/\[.*$/, "")
  dir = file.split("/")[0..2].join("/")
  t = rt.to_f
  groups[dir][:count] += 1
  groups[dir][:time] += t
  files[file][:count] += 1
  files[file][:time] += t
end
puts "=== BY DIR ==="
groups.sort_by { |_, v| -v[:time] }.each { |k, v| printf "%-30s %5d examples  %8.2fs\n", k, v[:count], v[:time] }
puts "\n=== TOP 30 FILES IN spec/requests ==="
files.select { |k, _| k.start_with?("./spec/requests") }.sort_by { |_, v| -v[:time] }.first(30).each do |k, v|
  printf "%-65s %4d examples  %8.2fs\n", k, v[:count], v[:time]
end
'

module SignedRequestHelpers
  def get(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "get #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")

    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end

  def post(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    headers['Digest'] = "SHA-256=#{Digest::SHA256.base64digest(args[:params].to_s)}"

    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end

module ProviderRequestHelper
  private

  def stub_provider_request(provider, path: '/', method: :get, response_status: 200, response_body: '')
    response_body = encode_body(response_body)
    response_headers = {
      'content-type' => 'application/json',
    }.merge(response_authentication_headers(provider, response_status, response_body))

    stub_request(method, provider.url(path))
      .to_return do |_request|
        {
          status: response_status,
          body: response_body,
          headers: response_headers,
        }
      end
  end

  def request_authentication_headers(provider, url: root_url, method: :get, body: '')
    body = encode_body(body)
    headers = {}
    headers['content-digest'] = content_digest(body)
    request = "Net::HTTP::#{method.to_s.classify}".constantize.new(URI(url), headers)
    key = private_key_for(provider)
    Linzer.sign!(request, key:, components: %w(@method @target-uri content-digest))
    signature_headers(request)
  end

  def response_authentication_headers(provider, status, body)
    response = Net::HTTPResponse::CODE_TO_OBJ[status.to_s].new('1.1', status, Rack::Utils::HTTP_STATUS_CODES[status])
    response.body = body
    response['content-digest'] = content_digest(body)
    key = private_key_for(provider)
    Linzer.sign!(response, key:, components: %w(@status content-digest))
    signature_headers(response)
  end

  def signature_headers(operation)
    {
      'content-digest' => operation['content-digest'],
      'signature-input' => operation['signature-input'],
      'signature' => operation['signature'],
    }
  end

  def private_key_for(provider)
    @cached_provider_keys ||= {}
    @cached_provider_keys[provider] ||=
      begin
        key = OpenSSL::PKey.generate_key('ed25519')
        provider.update!(provider_public_key_pem: key.public_to_pem)
        key
      end

    Linzer.new_ed25519_key(@cached_provider_keys[provider].private_to_pem, provider.id.to_s)
  end

  def encode_body(body)
    return body if body.nil? || body.is_a?(String)

    encoder = ActionDispatch::RequestEncoder.encoder(:json)
    encoder.encode_params(body)
  end

  def content_digest(content)
    "sha-256=:#{OpenSSL::Digest.base64digest('sha256', content)}:"
  end
end

**Holy Cow! This is a Factory Frenzy!**

Okay, stop everything! I need to process this. My jaw is on the floor. Look at these timings! We've got a serious bottleneck here. I'm seeing astronomical percentages of time being swallowed up by factories in these request specs.

First, in `cache_spec.rb`, a staggering 81.1% of the total time (50.87 seconds out of 62.69) is dedicated solely to factory instantiation. And we're talking about 258 examples, each diligently churning out a small army of fabricated objects: `status`, `bookmark`, `account`, `moderator_user`, `invite`, `poll`, `accessible_access_token`, and `login_activity` – all repeated *multiple* times per example!

Then, `activitypub` is somehow even *worse*: a mind-boggling 87.9% (47.81 seconds out of 54.39) is devoted to factories. And again, 108 examples are generating `status` and `bookmark` at such a high rate it’s causing BCrypt to be run multiple times (908 in activitypub alone, with only one top-level fabricated user!). Something is clearly VERY wrong here. This is especially alarming since every `Fabricate(:status)` also, for some reason, fabricates a `bookmark`. Seriously, *why*? 551 statuses = 551 bookmarks; 516 statuses = 516 bookmarks. That's bizarre.

Okay, deep breath. We need to understand this. We need to go straight to the source. Right now, I'm diving headfirst into `spec/fabricators/` – read-only, of course, no edits. We need to figure out why these factories are such resource hogs. I need to understand why `Fabricate(:status)`, `Fabricate(:user)`, and `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` are causing so much work. I'm also going to check `config/initializers/devise.rb`, `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb`, and `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb`! We need to understand these configuration, Sidekiq, BCrypt, `rails_helper`, shared-context, and setup elements so that we can have that "ah-ha" moment that leads to a full optimization for phase 2.

We can't touch the factories directly yet, but reading these files will provide invaluable insights for *both* our upcoming optimization phase *and* our documentation efforts for the factories phase! This is going to be incredibly insightful, I can feel it.

Okay, this is interesting. I'm seeing some clear patterns emerging from this analysis of the request specs. My immediate reaction is, "Wow, this is ripe for optimization!" Let me break down what's grabbing my attention:

This signals opportunities to refactor and DRY up test setup. Centralizing authentication logic into shared contexts or helper methods is practically screaming to be done.

2.  **Authorization Testing:** The frequency of `forbidden for wrong scope` and `forbidden for wrong role` examples (239 times!) tells me that authorization is a critical part of these tests, but it might be causing significant overhead. I need to dig deeper into the timing data to see if these are the main culprits. It looks like those examples are concentrated in `/tmp/requests_post_phase1.json`, which took 11.93s when using `./spec/support/examples/api.rb`, so let's check true per-file timing.

3.  **Route Reloading:** The presence of `reload_routes!` in both `signature_verification_spec.rb` (8.47s for 30 examples) and `csp_spec.rb` is concerning. Reloading routes can be a time-consuming operation, and it's something I need to evaluate if it's truly necessary in each of these files. Can we refactor these tests to avoid the reload or at least optimize its use?

4.  **Sidekiq Configuration Inconsistencies:** The inconsistent use of `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` versus `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` is a potential performance drain. Many specs manually use `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` ONLY when `have_enqueued_sidekiq_job` is used. With ~1,850 request examples running `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)`, it's a good idea to see if we can globally switch to `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)`. I'm curious if this offers a significant speedup. Let's see how many requests specs actually *need* `:inline_sidekiq` and if this change saves any noticeable time.

5.  **Overall Request Spec Performance:** I'm also really curious about the overall time taken by the tests, which, based on the non-profiler overhead, is around 72s. This should save considerable time. Specifically, I'm thinking that I can use a default token and only generate a new token if the user or scopes are overridden in a nested context. I also need to ensure that the code is safe with overridden `user` values, including nil. It seems like the existing code would have raised an error in some cases.

I'm also considering the `forbidden for wrong role` shared example from `api.rb`. I need to figure out how many times it's used and if I can avoid fabricating multiple users for the same role. I'm going to grep for this right now, as it's a huge potential win if the same user can be reused.

Third, I'm looking at Redis cleanup (`redis.flushdb`), `Rails.cache.clear`, and the signed request helpers. I need to quantify the time spent on these and whether there are opportunities for optimization. Specifically, I'll need to figure out how long RSA signing takes in `SignedRequestHelpers`. **Optimizing "forbidden for wrong role" in API Specs**

Okay, so I've stumbled upon something interesting while reviewing the API specs. It looks like the `forbidden for wrong role` shared example is used extensively. Let's see... a quick `grep` confirms it's called over 100 times! And each time, it's creating a brand new user, account, login activity, and keypair. This seems inefficient, especially when considering that `with API authentication` is already setting up a user.

The core issue is in how `forbidden for wrong role` is implemented. It fabricates a new user within each example. However,  `with API authentication` already establishes a user and I can simply update the user's role instead of creating a new one, which would be *much* faster. I'm talking about 0.2ms vs 25ms here, big difference!

I started to think about why this is happening. The key lies in `spec/support/examples/api.rb` and the interaction between the outer `before` blocks and the `it_behaves_like` contexts. Specifically, the comment in `api.rb`: `# Some examples have a subject which needs to be called to make a request / subject if request.nil?` and the fact that an HTTP request is sometimes made in an outer `before` block. This forces the lazy evaluation of `let(:user)` in `with API authentication`. The `forbidden for wrong role` example redefines `let(:user)` because it needs to control the user's role.

Now, how can we avoid this constant user fabrication? The obvious answer is to reuse the user created by `with API authentication`. The first instinct is using a `let_it_be` at the parent group level, but since `it_behaves_like` creates a child example group, a simple `let_it_be` there doesn't work.

But wait a minute! What if we use `super()` within the `let(:user)` in the `forbidden for wrong role` example?  Here's the plan. Inside the shared example, when `super()` is called within `let(:user)`, it should return the parent group's user. If the parent group is using `let_it_be(:user) { Fabricate(user_fabricator) }` then `super()` should be that user.  So, in the `forbidden for wrong role` example, inside `let(:user)`, we can now update the role of the user (e.g. `super().tap { |u| u.update!(role: role) }`)! This update occurs before any outer `before` block, and the transaction is rolled back at the end of the example!

The beauty of this is that it avoids any new fabrications! No new users, accounts, login activities, or tokens! The user from `with API authentication` gets reused. Also, the `refind: true` option of `let_it_be` ensures that the user is refreshed in the database for the next example.

Now, I need to double-check a couple of things. I need to make sure `super()` is always defined, and the user that `super()` returns is the one we want to act upon. Then, I need to search the entire `spec/` directory to check for cases where the target is not the `super()` user. If that's the case, we'll have to adapt. I'll take a quick look now.

The most glaring issue is the discrepancy between the time saved in `spec/requests` versus the impressive 96 seconds saved by that same configuration in `spec/models`. Something's clearly off. My instincts were correct: it all comes down to the setup in `spec/requests`.

A quick rewind to the `FactoryProf` numbers paints a clear picture. Across the board, `Fabricate(...)` is a major bottleneck:

1.  `spec/requests/api`: **58%** of the time spent is in `Fabricate(...)`!
2.  `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb`: **81%** of the time spent is in `Fabricate(...)`!
3.  `spec/requests/activitypub`: **88%** of the time spent is in `Fabricate(...)`!

Summing this up, out of the total 149 seconds run time for `spec/requests`, a significant portion – **65-70%** (about 95-105 seconds) – is just repeated per-example `Fabricate(...)` calls and setup operations, plus `reload_routes!`. The actual HTTP requests, the controller logic, views, the DB interaction, and per-example hooks? They're taking only about 45 seconds (24ms/request), combined.

This brings me to two optimization avenues:

1.  **Shared Setup**: First, consolidate all the repeated setups. The current setup, `spec/support/api_authentication.rb`, is used in 70 files. We can speed this up by migrating existing API test files to use the context and/or `let_it_be` to set up shared variables. We have a solid starting point with the shared examples like `forbidden for wrong role` and `forbidden for wrong scope`, and they're used in over 200 examples. Integrating `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` in `spec/rails_helper.rb` with the inline tag on those 8 files is critical to prevent unintended background job execution. We should also investigate if `TestProf::BeforeAll` might require a helper, like when `PostStatusService` is called (in cases where notifications/timelines are initialized through `before_all`).
2.  **Redis Cache and Flush**: The `config.after` block in `spec/rails_helper.rb` calls `Rails.cache.clear` and `redis.flushdb` after each example. I need to measure the speed of these calls. The implications here are *huge* because home timelines, trends, and various caches rely on Redis. Any `before_all` or `let_it_be` setups MUST *only* use PostgreSQL state. NEVER Redis or `Rails.cache` unless it is deliberately populated within a `before` block. This crucial rule will sidestep all sorts of flaky behavior due to ordering! The implementation in Phase 1 with the `trends/statuses_spec.rb` is an excellent example of this.

To make sure I'm not missing any other suite-wide hidden costs, I need to run a benchmark/profiler on the non-factory parts of `spec/requests`. We need to examine what is going on with the controller rendering, `Devise`, `Warden`, `Paperclip`, and other dependencies.

class ActivityPub::ContextsController < ActivityPub::BaseController
  vary_by -> { 'Signature' if authorized_fetch_mode? }

  before_action :require_account_signature!, if: :authorized_fetch_mode?
  before_action :set_conversation
  before_action :set_items

  DESCENDANTS_LIMIT = 60

  def show
    expires_in 3.minutes, public: public_fetch_mode?
    render_with_cache json: context_presenter, serializer: ActivityPub::ContextSerializer, adapter: ActivityPub::Adapter, content_type: 'application/activity+json'
  end

  def items
    expires_in 3.minutes, public: public_fetch_mode?
    render_with_cache json: items_collection_presenter, serializer: ActivityPub::CollectionSerializer, adapter: ActivityPub::Adapter, content_type: 'application/activity+json'
  end

  private

  def account_required?
    false
  end

  def set_conversation
    account_id, status_id = params[:id].split('-')
    @conversation = Conversation.local.find_by(parent_account_id: account_id, parent_status_id: status_id)
  end

  def set_items
    @items = @conversation.statuses.distributable_visibility.paginate_by_min_id(DESCENDANTS_LIMIT, params[:min_id])
  end

  def context_presenter
    first_page = ActivityPub::CollectionPresenter.new(
      type: :unordered,
      part_of: context_url(@conversation),
      next: next_page,
      items: @items.map { |status| status.local? ? ActivityPub::TagManager.instance.uri_for(status) : status.uri }
    )

    ActivityPub::ContextPresenter.from_conversation(@conversation).tap do |presenter|
      presenter.first = first_page
    end
  end

  def items_collection_presenter
    page = ActivityPub::CollectionPresenter.new(
      id: items_context_url(@conversation, page_params),
      type: :unordered,
      part_of: context_url(@conversation),
      next: next_page,
      items: @items.map { |status| status.local? ? ActivityPub::TagManager.instance.uri_for(status) : status.uri }
    )

    return page if page_requested?

    ActivityPub::CollectionPresenter.new(
      id: items_context_url(@conversation),
      type: :unordered,
      first: page
    )
  end

  def page_requested?
    truthy_param?(:page)
  end

  def next_page
    return nil if @items.size < DESCENDANTS_LIMIT

    items_context_url(@conversation, page: true, min_id: @items.last.id)
  end

  def page_params
    params.permit(:page, :min_id)
  end
end

**A Deep Dive into RSpec Context and Fabrication**

Okay, let's break this down. I've spotted a subtle issue in how we're using `include_context` with `let_it_be` and `let` in our API specs, specifically in `notifications_spec.rb` and others. The core problem is the execution order and the potential for premature fabrication of user objects.

Initially, `include_context 'with API authentication'` utilizes `let_it_be` to set up a `user` and `default_token`. This happens in a `before_all` block, before the spec file itself might override `let(:user)`. This is where it gets tricky. If the spec file *does* override `let(:user)`, the `default_token` could be fabricated using the *first* (un-overridden) `user` object.

Here's the rub: `let_it_be` registers a `before_all` hook that, in turn, may use a potentially outdated version of an object that's later being redefined. I need to be careful, because `let_it_be(:default_token)` calls `user.id` inside its own `before_all` block. Thus the first `before_all` in `with API authentication` might run and create a user. The second `before_all` block, also in `with API authentication`, calls `self.user` which at this point references the original value of user, which is then updated by a third `before_all`. This can lead to extra, unnecessary fabrications and, potentially, unexpected behavior.

I'm thinking we can address this to improve the clarity of `spec/support/api_authentication.rb`. The goal is to make it robust and cleaner. Two potential options emerge:

1.  We could support the `user_attributes: {}` inside `'with API authentication'`.
2.  We could modify how `token` memoizes on a class or group level.

The simpler answer, and my preferred one, is to leverage an `unless method_defined?(:user)` check within the shared context. This way, the shared context only fabricates its "default" user if the spec file *doesn't* already define `let_it_be(:user)` or `let(:user)`. An alternative way to implement this is to utilize the `**user_options` parameter passed to `include_context`. Then `spec/support/api_authentication.rb` would need to check for `method_defined?(:user)`.

Even better: using a `default_auth_user` and `default_auth_token`, plus `**user_options`, resolves all of this. Inside our `shared_context`, we could have:

RSpec.shared_context 'with API authentication' do |oauth_scopes: '', user_fabricator: :user|
  let_it_be(:default_auth_user)  { Fabricate(user_fabricator) }
  let_it_be(:default_auth_token) { Fabricate(:accessible_access_token, resource_owner_id: default_auth_user.id, scopes: oauth_scopes) }
  let(:user)                     { default_auth_user }
  let(:scopes)                   { oauth_scopes }
  let(:token) do
    if user&.id == default_auth_token.resource_owner_id
      default_auth_token.update!(scopes: scopes) if default_auth_token.scopes.to_s != scopes.to_s
      default_auth_token
    else
      Fabricate(:accessible_access_token, resource_owner_id: user.id, scopes: scopes)
    end
  let(:headers) { { 'Authorization' => "Bearer #{token.token}" } }
end

By doing this, most examples call `headers` and `token` and use `default_auth_user`, and we avoid extra fabrication. The `account` pattern in `profiles_spec.rb` avoids a crash. If we use `let_it_be(:default_auth_user)`, the `default_auth_user` is created with our desired attributes. This design should be the most robust and avoids crashes and extra fabrication. Let's make sure to review the entire Layer 1 notification specs.

We can solve this entire conundrum by allowing specs to control user creation, yet still benefit from a shared context. This looks like a complete fix, addressing potential bugs and optimizing our test setup.

**Optimizing Test Suite Performance: Batch 2A Analysis**

Okay, let's break down these performance optimizations for the test suite, specifically Batch 2A, focusing on reducing redundant database interactions and route reloads.

First, I need to zero in on `signature_verification_spec.rb`, specifically line 125. The code's structure sets up a "known account" with a Fabricated actor, and then, within a nested context, attempts to re-Fabricate an account with the same username and domain. My concern is that the unique index on `(username, domain)` in PostgreSQL could raise an `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` error. Thankfully, FactoryProf has shown that Fabricating accounts is comparatively fast (0.84s total) versus reloads. The solution is to move the controller setup and route reloading (`stub_tests_controller` and `Rails.application.reload_routes!`) from before/after each example (30x) to before(:all)/after(:all) (1x), along with pre-parsing `actor_keypair` once, which should significantly drop the test execution time from 8.47s to around 0.8s without introducing any risk of unique constraint issues.

Now, let's examine the other specs and identify potential improvements. I'm going through `cache_spec.rb`, `activitypub/replies_spec.rb`, `activitypub/contexts_spec.rb`, `activitypub/outboxes_spec.rb`, and `activitypub/collections_spec.rb` methodically.

In `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb`, I'll replace `let` with `let_it_be` for `alice`, `user`, and `token`, and move the setup code – Fabricating statuses, invite, poll, and follow relationship – into a single `before_all` block. This reduces redundant database operations across all 258 read-only examples.  Similar application will be done on the two `let_it_be` remote actors in the Signature-related contexts.

`spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb` needs a close examination. I see we have a `let_it_be(:status)`, `let_it_be(:remote_account)`, and `before_all` to create shared reply statuses. I need to make sure that the `before` block which stubs `DESCENDANTS_LIMIT` and modifies the visibility of the status, is accounted for. Particularly, the `let_it_be(:status)` has `refind: true` so the status and account are fresh in every example.

# RSpec Test Suite Profiling & Optimization Notes

## Benchmark Metrics (Single-Process, Default Exclusions: `~js ~search ~streaming`)

| Suite | Examples | Baseline (`2aa391f`) | After Phase 1 (`models`) | After Phase 2 (`requests`) | Speedup vs Baseline |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `spec/models` | 1,795 | 129.7s (2m 09.7s) | 33.1s – 35.5s | 35.5s | **-72.6% (3.65x faster)** |
| `spec/requests` | 1,877 | 172.1s (2m 52.1s) | 149.1s (2m 29.1s) | 65.9s (1m 05.9s) | **-61.7% (2.61x faster)** |
| **Combined (`models` + `requests`)** | **3,672** | **301.8s (5m 01.8s)** | **182.2s (3m 02.2s)** | **101.4s (1m 41.4s)** | **-66.4% (2.98x faster)** |

---

## Phase 1 Summary (`spec/models` + Global Test Environment)

1. **Test Logging (`config/environments/test.rb`)**: Set `config.log_level = ENV.fetch('RAILS_LOG_LEVEL', 'warn').to_sym` instead of `:debug` to avoid formatting/writing SQL and view logs on every example.
2. **Redis Cleanup (`spec/rails_helper.rb`)**: Replaced `redis.del(redis.keys)` with `redis.flushdb` in `config.after` (total cost ~0.10s across 1,877 examples).
3. **TestProf Integration (`spec/rails_helper.rb`)**: Enabled `before_all` and `let_it_be` (`default_modifiers[:refind] = true`), reloading persisted `let_it_be` ActiveRecord ivars on transaction rollback.
4. **Fake Sidekiq for Model Specs**: Switched `type: :model` specs from `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` to `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` by default, opting in with `:inline_sidekiq` only where inline worker side effects are asserted.
5. **Model Spec Shared Setup**: Converted top slow `spec/models` files to `let_it_be` / `before_all`.

---

## Phase 2 Summary (`spec/requests`)

### Profiling Findings on `spec/requests` (Post-Phase-1: 149.1s)

- **Factory/DB setup dominated runtime**:
  - `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb`: 30.16s (258 read-only `GET` examples; 81% of time spent fabricating identical records per example).
  - `spec/requests/api/**`: 72.22s across 1,073 examples; 58% of time spent in `Fabricate` (`user`: 802x / 19.6s, `status`: 272x / 14.1s, `account`: 470x / 11.2s, `bookmark`: 280x / 6.3s, `admin_user`: 216x / 5.2s, `login_activity`: 2,050x / 2.8s, `accessible_access_token`: 902x / 1.6s).
  - `spec/requests/activitypub/**`: 21.25s across 108 examples; 88% of time spent in `Fabricate` (`replies_spec.rb` alone was 13.89s, creating 7 statuses per example x 45 examples; `contexts_spec.rb` fabricated `DESCENDANTS_LIMIT = 60` statuses without stubbing the constant in `GET #show`).
  - `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb`: 8.47s across 30 examples, ~90% spent running `Rails.application.routes.draw` + `Rails.application.reload_routes!` per example.
- **Inline Sidekiq overhead**: Running `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` executed distribution, ActivityPub, notification, and mail workers unnecessarily on almost all 1,877 request examples; only 8 request spec files depended on inline Sidekiq (4 during HTTP execution, 4 only during notification/conversation test data setup).

### Optimizations Applied in Phase 2

1. **Default `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` for Request Specs (`spec/rails_helper.rb`)**:
   - Extended fake Sidekiq default to `%i(model request)`, tagging the 4 request contexts that test inline job side effects with `:inline_sidekiq` (`api/v1/admin/account_actions_spec.rb`, `api/v1/reports_spec.rb`, `api/v1/statuses/favourites_spec.rb`, `api/v1/timelines/home_spec.rb`) and wrapping `before_all` setup in `Sidekiq::Testing.inline!` for the 4 notification/conversation specs.
2. **Shared API Authentication & Authorization Examples (`spec/support/api_authentication.rb`, `spec/support/examples/api.rb`)**:
   - Converted `'with API authentication'` to create `default_auth_user` and `default_auth_token` once per group via `let_it_be`, updating `default_auth_token.scopes` in-transaction when `scopes` is overridden (eliminating user/token fabrication across 166 `'forbidden for wrong scope'` examples and ~700+ standard API examples).
   - Updated `'forbidden for wrong role'` (73 examples across admin API specs) to update `super()`'s `role_id` inside the rolled-back transaction instead of fabricating a new `User` + `Account` + `AccessToken` per example.
   - Migrated API request specs that manually duplicated the 4-line `user`/`scopes`/`token`/`headers` boilerplate to `include_context 'with API authentication'`.
3. **Pre-parsed Test RSA Private Key (`spec/support/signing_keys_helpers.rb`)**:
   - Parsed `PRIVATE_RSA_TEST_KEY` once into `PARSED_PRIVATE_RSA_TEST_KEY` instead of calling `OpenSSL::PKey.read` on every signed ActivityPub request.
4. **Targeted Shared Setup (`let_it_be` / `before_all`) in Top Slow Request Specs**:
   - `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb`: 30.16s -> 5.80s
   - `spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb`: 13.89s -> 2.79s
   - `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb`: 8.47s -> ~0.5s (moved route drawing/reloading to `before_all`/`after(:all)`)
   - `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb`: 7.95s -> 1.85s
   - `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb`: 5.32s -> 2.18s
   - `spec/requests/activitypub/contexts_spec.rb`: 3.17s -> <0.5s (plus consistent `DESCENDANTS_LIMIT` stubbing)
   - Additional read-heavy specs (`timelines/{public,link,tag}_spec.rb`, `activitypub/{outboxes,collections}_spec.rb`, `accounts_spec.rb`, `statuses_spec.rb`, `statuses/activity_spec.rb`, `api/v1/statuses_spec.rb`, `api/v1/statuses/quotes_spec.rb`, `api/v1/accounts/statuses_spec.rb`, `api/v1/admin/{accounts,reports}_spec.rb`, `api/v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb`).

---

## Important Caveats for Future Optimization Phases

1. **Redis & `Rails.cache` Reset Per Example**:
   `spec/rails_helper.rb` runs `Rails.cache.clear` and `redis.flushdb` in `config.after`. Never rely on Redis data (e.g., `FeedManager` home timelines, `Trends::*`) or `Rails.cache` populated in `before_all` surviving past the first example. Keep PostgreSQL record creation in `before_all` and Redis population in `before`.
2. **Sidekiq Mode Inside `before_all`**:
   `TestProf::BeforeAll` forces `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` before `:begin`. If `before_all` calls a service (e.g., `PostStatusService`, `FavouriteService`) that creates required PostgreSQL records (`Notification`, `AccountConversation`) via Sidekiq workers, wrap that setup block in `Sidekiq::Testing.inline! { ... }`.
3. **Paperclip Disk Attachments**:
   Paperclip stores test uploads under `spec/test_files/` and only cleans them up in `after(:suite)`. Avoid sharing a single `let_it_be` record across examples that delete attachments on disk (e.g., `DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar`) when sibling examples assert `expect(account.avatar).to exist`.
4. **Devise Virtual `password` Attribute**:
   `let_it_be` with `refind: true` reloads `User` via `User.find(id)`, where virtual `user.password` is `nil`. Specs that post `user.password` to `user_session_path` need either a fresh `Fabricate(:user)` or an explicit password string.
5. **Snowflake ID Ordering**:
   Pagination endpoints order by `id DESC` (Snowflake IDs). When converting mixed `let` / `let!` setups to `let_it_be`, preserve declaration order so `min_id` / `max_id` pagination link assertions see the same relative IDs.

---

## Plan & High-Value Targets for Next Phase: Factories (`spec/fabricators/`)

FactoryProf across the optimized `spec/requests` suite shows dramatic remaining upside inside `spec/fabricators/` (which will simultaneously speed up `models`, `requests`, `controllers`, `services`, `workers`, and `serializers`):

1. **`spec/fabricators/status_fabricator.rb` (Highest Priority)**:
   ```ruby
   after_create do |status|
     Fabricate(:bookmark, status: status)
   end
   ```
   Every single `Fabricate(:status)` unconditionally creates a `Bookmark`, which in turn fabricates a new `Account` -> `User` (BCrypt hash) -> 2 `LoginActivity` rows! In `spec/requests` alone, 331 of 340 `bookmark` fabrications (4.55s) are collateral from `Fabricate(:status)`. Removing this `after_create` hook (and explicitly creating bookmarks in any spec that actually tests bookmark presence/cascade deletion) will cut `Fabricate(:status)` time by more than half suite-wide.
2. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb`**:
   ```ruby
   after_create do |user|
     2.times { Fabricate(:login_activity, user: user) }
   end
   ```
   Every `Fabricate(:user)` (and every local `Fabricate(:account)`) inserts 2 `LoginActivity` records. Moving this to a dedicated trait/fabricator or removing it where unused eliminates thousands of SQL `INSERT`s across the test suite. Pre-computing BCrypt's `encrypted_password` for the default `'123456789'` password (when `password` is not overridden) can also shave BCrypt CPU overhead.
3. **`spec/fabricators/account_fabricator.rb`**:
   Local `:account` always builds an associated `:user` (`user { |attrs| attrs[:domain].nil? ? Fabricate.build(:user, account: nil) : nil }`). Investigating whether `:account` always requires `:user` (or optimizing `:user` first so `:account` automatically becomes cheap) will reduce the ~14–25ms per-account cost.
4. **Attachment Fabricators (`media_attachment_fabricator.rb`, `custom_emoji_fabricator.rb`)**:
   Each `media_attachment` (~53ms) and `custom_emoji` (~46ms) runs Paperclip/libvips metadata & style processing; stubbing post-processing or using minimal 1x1 fixtures where dimensions/thumbnails are not under test can cut attachment factory cost significantly.
EOF

I have profiled and optimized the `spec/requests` test suite while preserving all example assertions, keeping `spec/fabricators/` and runtime application code untouched, and storing baseline metrics, profiling insights, caveats, and future optimization plans in `docs/RSPEC_OPTIMIZATION.md`.

### Results Summary

| Suite | Examples | Pre-Optimization Baseline (`HEAD`) | After Phase 1 (`models`) | After Phase 2 (`requests`) | Change vs Baseline |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `spec/models` | 1,795 | 129.7s (2m 09.7s) | 33.1s – 35.5s | 35.5s | **-72.6% (3.65x faster)** |
| `spec/requests` | 1,877 | 172.1s (2m 52.1s) | 149.1s (2m 29.1s) | **65.9s (1m 05.9s)** | **-61.7% (2.61x faster)** |
| **Combined (`models` + `requests`)** | **3,672** | **301.8s (5m 01.8s)** | **182.2s (3m 02.2s)** | **101.4s (1m 41.4s)** | **-66.4% (2.98x faster)** |

### Key Changes Made

1. **Default `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` for Request Specs (`spec/rails_helper.rb`)**:
   - Enabled `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` by default for `type: :request` (matching `type: :model`), adding `:inline_sidekiq` tags to the 4 request contexts that assert on inline worker side effects (`api/v1/admin/account_actions_spec.rb`, `api/v1/reports_spec.rb`, `api/v1/statuses/favourites_spec.rb`, `api/v1/timelines/home_spec.rb`) and wrapping `before_all` notification/conversation setup in `Sidekiq::Testing.inline!`.
2. **Shared API Authentication & Authorization Helpers (`spec/support/api_authentication.rb`, `spec/support/examples/api.rb`, `spec/support/signing_keys_helpers.rb`)**:
   - Updated `'with API authentication'` to share `default_auth_user` and `default_auth_token` via `let_it_be` (updating `scopes` in-transaction when overridden, e.g., in the 166 `'forbidden for wrong scope'` examples) and migrated duplicated 4-line OAuth setup blocks in API request specs to `include_context 'with API authentication'`.
   - Updated `'forbidden for wrong role'` (73 admin API examples) to update `super()`'s `role_id` inside the rolled-back example transaction instead of fabricating a new user, account, and token per example.
   - Pre-parsed `PRIVATE_RSA_TEST_KEY` once in `SigningKeysHelpers` instead of calling `OpenSSL::PKey.read` on every signed request.
3. **Shared Setup (`let_it_be` / `before_all`) in Top Bottleneck Request Specs**:
   - Restructured repeated per-example setup into `before_all` / `let_it_be` in the heaviest request specs (`cache_spec.rb`: 30.2s → 5.8s; `activitypub/replies_spec.rb`: 13.9s → 2.8s; `signature_verification_spec.rb`: 8.5s → ~0.5s by moving route drawing/reloading to `before_all`/`after(:all)`; `api/v2/notifications_spec.rb`: 8.0s → 1.9s; `api/v1/notifications_spec.rb`: 5.3s → 2.2s; `activitypub/contexts_spec.rb`: 3.2s → <0.5s; plus timeline, ActivityPub, account, status, and admin specs).
4. **Documentation (`docs/RSPEC_OPTIMIZATION.md`)**:
   - Recorded baseline and phase metrics, profiling breakdowns, architectural caveats for `before_all`/`let_it_be` (per-example Redis/`Rails.cache` resets, Paperclip disk files, Devise virtual `password`, Snowflake ID ordering), and high-priority targets for the upcoming factories optimization phase.

Issuing the final submission command now.

Fifth, the performance is exactly what I was aiming for. The `spec/requests` runtime is vastly improved. We're talking a reduction from the baseline of 172.1s (and 149.1s after Phase 1) down to 65.9s, which is a significant speed-up, a 61.7% decrease in runtime and a speed-up of 2.61x! The combined runtime of `spec/models` + `spec/requests` is down from 301.8s to roughly 101.4s, which represents a nearly 3x improvement, so a successful completion in that regard.

Finally, I made sure all the baseline metrics, insights from profiling, architectural caveats, and the roadmap for future factory optimizations are carefully documented in `docs/RSPEC_OPTIMIZATION.md`. It's all there for the next person to pick up.
